Let data1 be your target data, and data 2 be

Id2NameMap_unique(data2[,1:2])

dimnames(Id2NameMap)[[1]]_as.character(Id2NameMap[,1]) 

data1[,2]_Id2NameMap[as.character(data1[,2]),2]

--------------------------------------------------

 

Hope this help.

Max Zhao

messages.body_plain:
Rich,

I think your idea would run into problem for visualization when the scale of
y1 and y2 are very different.
For example, if y1 represents the sales volume in the range of 5000 -7000,
while y2 represents the winning percentage in the range of 20%-40%.  Then
letting ylim=c(20,7000) will squeeze the y2, impossible to view the changes
in y2.

In this case we still want to put them in a graph, we can use the artificial
scale on the right handside (i.e. add axis(side=4)). We can plot y1 vs. x
first, then map the y2 to the scale of y1 and the yticks for y1 to new
yticks for axis at side 4, and then add the axis for y2 at side 4.

Max

messages.subject_clean: Ref: Query on sandwich estimator -- Summary
messages.body_plain:
I'd like to THNAK the following people [ Jim Pratt,
Simon Rosenfeld, Eric Zivot, Andy Liam, Sundar
Dorai-Raj ] for their input and suggestions.

GOOGLE helped, along with the following responses.

Jim Pratt wrote:

The place I came across it some time ago was win the
context of GEE (Generalized Estiamting Equations). 
Its been awhile, but I recall it being the standard
error estimate coming from a Taylor's approximation.

Good luck.

Simon Rosenfeld wrote:

Sandwich estimator is a pretty wide concept. In a
simple context of regression models, sandwich
estimator is an asymptotically unbiased,
distribution-free estimator for variance of regression
coefficients.  
The best discussion I know may be found in McCullagh &
Nelder Generalized linear models 

See also Encyclopedia of Biostatistics

Hope it helps

Eric Zivot wrote:  

One type of sandwich estimator is used to compute an
estimate of the estimated coefficient variance matrix
from maximum likelihood estimation. If the likelihood
function is correctly specified then the inverse of
the empirical Hessian is used to estimate the
covariance matrix. If there is thought to be some
mispecification of the likelihood then in some cases 
the covariance matrix can be estimated using a
"sandwhich" estimator that utilizes both the gradient
and the Hessian of the log-likelihood. This
sandwich estimator is robust to certain types of
misspecification of the log-likelihood. I believe that
the optmin function in the MASS library 
has an option for computing a sandwich estimator.

messages.subject: Re: Standard file extensions
messages.body_plain:
ESS, Emacs Speaks Statistics, recognizes
.s .ssc .q .r .S .SSC .Q .R
as extensions for the S language.  ESS recognizes these extensions in the
sense that the editing environment---choice of keyword recognition and
highlighting, indentation styles, and interaction with running S language
processors (S-Plus or R)---is chosen based on these extensions.

The .r and .R extensions are primarily used for R, the others for S-Plus.

As Dr. Ripley points out, the Unix default is to use .s for assembler.
ESS overrides that default.

.s stands for S language
.q stands for QPE, quantitative programming environment
.ssc stands for S script.  This is the default extension used by the S-Plus 6 
GUI.

ESS recommends .st for S transcripts and .rt for R transcripts.  Again, we made
editing environment decisions based on these extensions.  For transcripts, we 
highlight
the syntax, recognize the prompts, and interact with the language processor.  
For example,
if the cursor is placed anywhere in a multiline transcript command (with the 
primary and
continuation prompts), and the enter key is pressed, then the entire multiline
command (without the prompts) is sent to the language processor.

The extensions .cmd .out .txt are generic and are not automatically assigned by 
emacs to
any language environment.

ESS is available at
         http://ESS.R-project.org

Information is at
Rossini, A.J., Richard M. Heiberger, Rodney Sparapani, Martin
MÃchler, and Kurt Hornik (2004).  ``Emacs Speaks Statistics (ESS): A
Multiplatform, Multipackage Development Environment for Statistical
Analysis,'' Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics,
13, 1, pp. 247â261.

messages.body_plain:
Dear S list members,

I have a dataframe called mydata with column names
  c("y1", ...,"y400","group","male","age","Education.Level")

I wrote a loop to run a series of regressions with response variables 
y1, ..., y400 respectively but the same predictors. For example,

result<- rep(NA,400)
dataset1<- mydata[,c(401:404)]
for (i in 1:400)
{dataset1$y<- mydata[,i]
 x<- lm(y ~ group + male + age + Education.Level,
        data=dataset1, na.action=na.exclude)
 result[i]<- summary(x)$coefficients[2,4]
}

However, due to large number of missing values in y, some of the 
computed fits are singular and thus terminate the loop. How could I 
modify the S code so that it assigns NA to result[i] whenever it happens 
and jump to the next model fitting in the loop? For example, if model 
for y5 is singular, then I will assign result[5] as NA and continue the 
loop to fit y6, ..., y400? Your help is highly appreciated!

Peng Huang

messages.body_plain:
I want to do a simple edit on a data frame of many factors. The edit is:
for 3 of the factors, I need to exclude observations that contain levels
below a certain frequency.

d <-
data.frame(x1=sample(1:10,rep=T,40),x2=sample(1:10,rep=T,40),x3=sample(1
:10,rep=T,40))

for(i in 1:3) 
    d[,i]<-factor(d[,i])[,drop=T]

apply(d,2,function(x){min(table(x))})
x1 x2 x3 
2   1  2

The minimum frequency of levels of x1 and x3 is 2, and is 1 for x2. The
edit I need in this example is to elevate that minimum to 4 for x1, x2,
x3 simultaneously. Now, 

x1.freq <- table(d$x1)
x1.retain <- names(x1.freq[x1.freq>3])
x1.retain
[1] "2"  "3"  "4"  "8"  "10"

d<-d[is.element(d$x1, x1.retain),]

By doing this we retain a minimum of 4 for levels of x1. We can then do
the same for x2. But editing x2 will entail loosing observations from
levels of x1 that we previously edited. Consequently, the minimum of 4
that we achieved in x1 will be lost in the process. This will further be
complicated by editing x3.

I performed the editing for x1, x2, then x3, iteratively until a minimum
of 4 obs/level was met for all three factors. The approach is cumbersome
and might not be correct, i.e., perhaps I deleted more than what I
needed to. 

Step1: 
Do editing for x1, followed by x2, then x3 as described above.

Step2: 
If(min(apply(d,2,function(x){min(table(x))})) < 4) Go To Step1; 
Else Exit

Any idea how can I achieve this cleanly and/or correctly.

Thanks

Gamal Abdel-Azim

messages.subject: Re: smoothing
messages.body_plain:
S-PLUS has built-in facilities for most, if not all, of what 
you're asking for.  ksmooth() gives you kernel smoother, I believe with 
choices of kernels.  (By `mean' I guess you meant the boxcar, or uniform, 
kernel).  Median smoothers are only appropriate for equally spaced data, 
and are difficult to compare with other smoothers.  You can get more 
sophisticated resistant smoothers with smooth().  LOESS is available via 
lowess() and loess().  

 

If 
you read a book on smoothing, you should find that the choice of kernel matters 
quite little.  Even though the quadratic kernel is theoretically optimal 
for MSE, there are practical reasons for choosing other 
kernels.

 

Not 
sure why you would want to leave more than one data point out in 
cross-validating smoothers.  I believe the literature generally prefer 
plug-in type bandwidth selection over CV.

 

Bias 
and variance can only be assessed if you know the truth function.  I guess 
you are referring to the Figure 2.2 on page 12 of Hastie & Tibshirani's 
book.  That's not difficult to generate from simulation: a single for 
loop will do.  The bias and variance can be drawn using polygon().  
This sort of things is mostly used for demonstration/teaching, not for analyzing 
real data.

 

HTH,

Andy

>I need to perform the two-sample paired t-test where the samples to
>be compared are the mixtures of normals sharing the same mean but
>differing by their variances.
>
>More specifically, suppose that the sample X contains n1 terms drawn
>from N(mu, sigma1), n2 terms drawn from N(mu, sigma2), etc. The
>sample Y has the same structure. I need to test the null hypothesis
>of equality of means, mu.X=mu.Y, and assign a p-value. Obviously, the
>X & Y are not normally distributed, and t-statistic is not
>t-distributed. Is there a general approach for performing something
>like t-test in this setting? Note: it is not a Behrens-Fisher
>problem, it is something different. Any ideas/references/software
>implementations are highly appreciated.

Are n1, n2, ... fixed?
If the null hypothesis is correct, then do the terms in Y have
the same variances as the corresponding terms in X?

If the answer to both questions is yes, then I suggest using a
a stratified permutation test.  This does not require that the
strata sizes in X and Y be identical.

If you have a data frame with variables "values", "treatment", "strata"
where values contains the numerical values, treatment has two levels
indicating sample X or Y, and strata = j for the observations
with variance sigmaj, then
        permutationTestMeans(data, treatment = treatment, group = strata)
would do it.  Example using artificial data is below.

This requires S+Resample; see the bottom of this message.

You could also use a different statistic; rather than a simple
average of the values within each treatment, take a weighted
mean of the strata means, with weights on the strata means
proportional to stratum size / estimated stratum variance.
The permutationTestMeans function doesn't support this, but the
more general permutationTest2 funtion would.

messages.body_plain:
Hello, I have a perplexing problem that I wonder if any of you can help me 
with.

I am trying to reconstruct daily average temperature in the Sacramento 
River basin over a ~30 year period.  There are about a dozen gaging 
stations at which temperature is recorded, but most of them started fairly 
recently.  Going back in time there are fewer and fewer, until at the 
beginning of the record there is only one; furthermore, even during periods 
when a given gage was online, there are numerous data gaps ranging from a 
day to years.

Temperature at the station furthest up the river is determined partly by 
temperature in the reservoir, which is a seasonal function of air 
temperature and water stored in the reservoir, with a change in that 
relationship in the mid-1990s.  Temperature at any other location is a 
function of air temperature, upstream temperature, river kilometer, and 
flow, but also strongly influenced at the more downstream locations by 
flows from tributaries.  I would prefer to model this without having to 
take flow into account, since with flow and tributary input the picture 
gets very messy (since the tribs are in the same basin the temperature 
patterns tend to be similar, in that warm periods are warm 
everywhere).  Correlations between stations are higher for closer stations 
but fairly high even for distant stations (e.g., ~0.85 for stations >200 km 
apart; the total distance is 420 km), except that the seasonal pattern just 
below the dam is different from that further downstream - not only less 
variable but the peak occurs at the end of the dry summer rather than in 
the middle of summer.

So my objective would be to take this ~10,000 X 12 data matrix with mostly 
missing values (esp. toward the beginning) and fill in the missing 
values.  I would like to try to capture as much of the short-term 
variability as possible (my main interest is thermal effects on salmon), 
and that variability is typically reflected in the data from all of the 
stations.  So the algorithm I would like to develop (or scrounge) would 
rely first on relationships with nearby stations, next on more distant 
stations, and finally on some kind of periodic spline (supplied a few years 
ago by Henrik Nielsen).  However, there is no one station that has a 
complete record, so this would have to be done adaptively.

Any ideas of how to do this - especially ones that don't involve brute force?

Thank you

Wim

I am working with large financial data sets (several GB's) for a research
project.  The data have three natural indices: time (e.g., month/year),
asset/company (e.g., IBM), and measurement (e.g., price or return).

Let's assume for simplicity that the data are all numeric.  Since the data
are naturally three-dimensional in the above sense, we might think about
storing the data in a three-dimensional array in S-PLUS.  We might also
think about "stacking" the data, say by asset, into a two-dimensional data
frame, with an added (factor) variable to indicate the asset.  (Example:

Date Price Asset
01/99  2.45 abc
02/99  2.56 abc
01/99 10.45 xyz
02/99 10.47 xyz

)

My question: for large amounts of data, which of these setups is generally

function.  This is analogous to fitting polynomial regressions of increasing

Is this alternative strategy reasonable?

messages.subject: Summary: Efficiency of arrays vs. data frames for large data sets
messages.subject_clean: Summary: Efficiency of arrays vs. data frames for large data sets
messages.body_plain:
First, thanks to all of you who replied to my question. I am summarizing the
responses here, as several people were interested in the answer.  The
original question is included below for reference.

Second, I apologize for the confusion my example created.  I gave price and
return as examples of measurements.  I did not intend to indicate that I
only had price and/or return as measurements.  I have about 50 numeric
variables derived from the CRSP and Compustat databases for each asset.

As for the issue of arrays vs. data frames, the answer really depends on how
regular the data are, i.e., do we have roughly equal amounts of data for
each asset.  Let's assume for the second that for each asset we have roughly
the same amount of data (e.g., in a 5-year period most of the assets under
investigation have about 5-years of data).

In this case, the array will be more efficient (in general), as Patrick
Burns and Scott Chasalow pointed out.  This is mostly due to the way arrays
are organized in memory, if I understand things correctly.  Scott Chasalow
also pointed out the advantage of being able to subscript more directly:  if
the dimnames of the array contain the dates, asset names, and measurement
names, respectively, it is generally faster to do things like

A[ ,"XYZ", ]

than 

B[is.element(B[, "Asset"], "XYZ"), ]

not only because of the memory organization, but also because the lengths of
the vector we match against are shorter in the array case (number of assets
vs. number of assets * number of dates, for example).

Finally, let's discuss the case of data with unequal histories.  With the
array, we will have to do a lot of padding with NA's because of the
structure of an array.  With the data frame, we don't need all those NA's.
So, if the amount of padding needed in the array is fairly large, the data
frame will be faster in general simply because it is the smaller object.

I hope my summary is accurate and is helpful to others.  If I have misspoke,
please correct me.

Once again, thanks for all your help.

Chris Green
Graduate Student, Statistics
University of Washington

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question on how to set up a bootstrapping problem in S-Plus (v. 
6.2.1 on Windows).  The basic problem involves survey data.   Each 
survey respondent was asked to rate 20 messages about a product on, 
let's say, a 0/1 scale where 1 is agree.  There are 30 products.  My 
client found the proportion of respondents who agreed (a "1") with the 
message for a product and then averaged over the 20 messages to create a 
single score for all the messages for that product.  He repeated this 
for all 30 products.  He did this in 2002 and 2003.  He asked me to 
calculate the standard errors and do a test to see if the score in 2003 
differs from the score in 2002 for each product.  The answers will 
determine compensation for management.

I want to do a bootstrap to calculate the standard errors and the mean 
scores and then use these to test the difference.  I set up a simple 
bootstrap is S using

       bootstrap(data.test, mean(apply(data.test, 2, mean)))

where data.test is a data frame of three randomly generated messages 
coded as  0/1 numbers (the columns) with 20 "respondents".  This 
represents just a single product.  The mean was used since the mean of 
the 0/1 data is just the sample proportion.  The actual data, when I get 
it, will have 20 messages and several thousand respondents for each of 
the 30 products.

This call to bootstrap gave me what I think I need, but since I've used 
this function so infrequently and am not that familiar with bootstrap, I 
need clarification on what it's doing.  I believe it's resampling 
data.test, then passing the resampled data frame to the function 
mean(apply...)).  Is this correct?  Based on the description above of 
what the client did, is this function giving me what I want?  Can I do a 
simple hypothesis test using the results?  Can I assume normality for 
that test?  Is there anything else I need to consider?

Thanks for any help or advice,

Walt Paczkowski
